A few miles beyond the village of **[[Doobius House]]**, in the wooded interior of [[The Outback]], something ancient has emerged from beneath the earth.

For months, hunters and woodsmen have whispered about a stone doorway that appeared at the foot of a grassy hill beyond the forest. No storm uncovered it. No landslide exposed it. One morning, it simply existed. The doorway stands beside an overgrown trail once used by hunters and woodsmen traveling through the forest.

A dozen adventurers have entered since.

Only one returned.

Half-starved and barely coherent, the survivor spoke of stone guardians, corpses crawling from their tombs, and terrible glass vessels filled with swirling darkness.

But one detail disturbed the people of [[Doobius House]] more than any other.

He swore that after his companions died, **he could still hear them screaming from inside the tomb.**

The tomb is the hidden laboratory of **[[Dopendis Gravebreath]]**, a necromancer and arcanist of [[Orcus]] who discovered a means of capturing mortal souls and storing them within enchanted vessels. Dopendis Gravebreath was supplied by a hidden Orcus cult operating among Stickyickistan’s mining interests; the cult sought to turn the island’s abundant [[Arcanite]] into a power source for a mass raise dead ritual.

Dopendis Gravebreath has disappeared.

His experiments have not.

# Adventure Hook

The characters begin at the [[FLS Guildhall]] on [[Nevercough Island]], looking for work through the [[Free League of Stickyickistan]]. A public notice on [[The Rolling Papers]] offers **150 gp** to investigate a newly revealed tomb in the wooded interior of [[The Outback]] and return with evidence of its purpose.

The notice explains that several explorers, hunters, and woodsmen from [[Doobius House]] entered the tomb after its discovery and never returned. Their sole survivor, **Bongston Vale**, was found half-starved and raving about black ceramic jars filled with screaming souls. He is recovering in the guildhall’s [[FLS Guildhall#Recovery support|recovery quarters]] and can be questioned before the party leaves.

Their families have contacted the Guildhall, desperate to learn what happened to them. A scholar working with [[The Seekers of the Vein]] has also taken an interest in the tomb because its stonework contains traces of refined [[Arcanite]], suggesting that someone transported valuable material deep into the forest. After hearing Bongston’s account, the families of the missing urge the characters to **free any souls they find**, not sell the jars or leave the dead trapped inside them.

Bongston remembers little clearly, but repeatedly warns:

> "Don't touch the jars. Gods above, don't touch the jars."

He remembers seeing his companions die, and then hearing their voices begging him for help from somewhere deeper inside the tomb.

237|Apparently, Dopendis Gravebreath intended to gather hundreds, perhaps thousands, of souls to power a ritual.
238|
239|Exactly what that ritual would accomplish isn't explained.
240|
241|Dopendis Gravebreath's current whereabouts are unknown.
242|
243|---
244|
245|# 6. West Libraries
246|
247|The southern library has collapsed.
248|
249|The northern chamber remains intact but locked.
250|
251|The door requires a **DC 13 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand using Thieves' Tools)** check or can simply be destroyed.
252|
253|> [!read-aloud] Read Aloud
254|> The chamber beyond is a preserved records room. Shelves hold stacks of brittle journals, rolled architectural plans, and thin metal plates etched with diagrams. Most of the notes concern the tomb itself: its hidden entrances, sealed doors, guardian chambers, and the illusion that concealed the structure from the outside world. Diagrams show magical lines running through the floors and walls, all converging on the central ritual chamber.
255|>
256|> A large map has been pinned above a writing desk. It shows the tomb’s rooms and protective enchantments, with several sections crossed out and rewritten in a different hand. One note explains that the concealment enchantment was designed to last for decades, but the ink beneath it has faded over a long period of time. Near the doors to the central chamber, one word has been written in large letters: **SYVETHIS**.
257|
258|Inside are records describing the tomb's magical protections.
259|
260|Characters learn that Dopendis Gravebreath concealed the entire structure using an enormous illusion and transmutation ritual.
261|
262|The enchantment was designed to last for decades.
263|
264|The tomb's recent appearance means the spell has finally failed.
265|
266|More importantly, they discover the command used to enter Dopendis Gravebreath's ritual chamber:
267|
268|## SYVETHIS
269|
270|Speaking the word near the doors in Area 2 causes ancient mechanisms to grind beneath the floor.
271|
272|The central doors slowly open.
273|
274|---
275|
276|# 7. Ritual Chamber
277|
278|The doors open onto an enormous circular chamber.
279|
280|Broken ritual equipment covers the floor.
281|
282|Black candles have melted into strange shapes.
283|
284|Silver wire forms incomplete magical circles.
285|
286|And surrounding the central ritual platform are **four active Jars of Souls**.
287|
288|Unlike the two inert vessels in Area 3, these jars are connected to the ritual machinery and actively distill Soul Diesel: a mixture of trapped souls and humanoid blood. The ritual machinery feeds the concentrate into the undead guardians, empowering them while keeping the souls conscious and trapped.
289|
290|Ghostly figures visibly swirl within the dark liquid.
291|
292|Some pound desperately against the inside of the glass.
293|
294|Among them are the souls of the adventurers who disappeared from [[Doobius House]]. As the characters enter, spectral guardians rise from the floor.
295|
296|
297|> [!read-aloud] Read Aloud
298|> The doors open onto an enormous circular chamber where the air feels heavy and strangely warm. Broken ritual equipment covers the floor, mixed with melted black candles and lengths of silver wire that form incomplete circles across the stone. At the center stands a raised ritual platform, its surface stained dark and marked with the remains of old magical symbols.
299|>
300|> Four glass Jars of Souls stand around the platform, each connected to the ritual circle by silver wires. Ghostly figures swirl within them, pressing their hands and faces against the glass. Some of the spirits look like the missing adventurers from [[Doobius House]]. Their silent mouths form desperate pleas, but no sound escapes the vessels.
301|>
302|> As you step into the chamber, the wires begin to glow. The jars pulse with cold light, and the shadows beneath the platform move independently of the objects that cast them. A skeletal hand punches through the stone beside the platform. Then another. Bones claw their way upward as a figure in a stained alchemist’s coat pulls itself from the floor. Glass vials clatter against its ribcage, and a cracked skull turns toward you, empty eye sockets burning with pale blue light. The skeleton raises one hand, and the silver wires snap taut as though answering its command, and two more spectral figures rise from the floor beside the Skeleton.
303|
304|### Encounter
305|
306|Use:
307|
308|**2 Specters**
309|
310|and
311|
312|**1 Skeletal Alchemist**
313|
314|The Skeletal Alchemist wears a stained alchemist’s coat and carries glass vials filled with corrosive fluid. It acts as the ritual chamber’s physical caretaker, using acid to drive intruders away from the active jars.
315|
316|The Skeleton and Specters are bound spirits forced to defend the laboratory.
317|
318|### Soul Diesel-Fueled Guardians
319|
320|The active jars pump Soul Diesel through the silver wires and into the undead guardians. The Specters and Skeletal Alchemist are under the strain’s effects.
321|
322|**Soul Diesel.** Once per turn, when a Specter or the Skeletal Alchemist deals damage to a humanoid with an attack, it deals an extra **1d4 damage of the same type as the attack**. The bonus damage is part of the attack’s damage and does not apply against creatures that are not humanoids.
323|
324|At **Initiative Count 20**, one intact active jar emits a pulse of necrotic energy. One undead creature in the tomb gains **5 Temporary Hit Points**. The characters can prevent this by destroying the active jars during combat.
325|
326|Roll 1d4 to determine which active jar pulses. If the number rolled was assigned to a jar that has been destroyed, nothing happens.
327|
328|### Breaking an Active Jar
329|
330|AC 12  
331|HP 10
332|
333|When an active jar is destroyed, its trapped souls erupt outward and the ritual machinery discharges through the vessel. Every creature within 5 feet must make a **DC 12 Wisdom saving throw**, taking **2d6 Psychic damage** on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. A creature that fails the save is also **Frightened for 1 minute**. It can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success.
334|
335|Every undead creature within 5 feet takes **1d6 Radiant damage** as the jar’s necrotic energy collapses. The spirits then disappear. A character proficient in Arcana or Religion realizes that the souls have finally been allowed to pass into the afterlife.
336|
337|Destroying an active jar weakens the ritual and prevents it from empowering the undead at Initiative Count 20. This gives the players an important tactical choice: fight the guardians normally, or smash the very artifacts they came to investigate.
338|
339|---

48|> **“Touch the jars. Bring me every one you can carry.”**
49|
50|Skarguther pays **300 gp per intact active jar** and **100 gp per intact inert jar**. The four active jars in the ritual chamber are worth **1,200 gp** total, and the two inert jars in Area 3 are worth **200 gp** total, for a possible maximum payment of **1,400 gp** if all six jars are recovered intact. To collect, deliver the jars to the Dungsweepers’ mortuary offices in [[The Undercity Osslurraggath]] and give the clerk the notice or the phrase **“The dead are still moving.”** Broken jars and released souls earn no payment. The public 100 gp reward remains available, but this contract asks the characters to collect the jars rather than smash them.
51|
52|---
53|
54|# Reaching the Tomb
55|
56|The tomb lies roughly **two days from [[Doobius House]]** through dense forest.
57|
58|The journey doesn't need to be a full wilderness adventure. Instead, use it to establish the increasingly unnatural atmosphere surrounding the tomb.
59|
60|During the second day, animals become scarce.
61|
62|Birdsong disappears.
63|
64|That evening, characters occasionally hear whispers between the trees.
65|
66|A character who succeeds on a **DC 12 Wisdom (Perception)** check hears fragments:
67|
68|_"Come closer..."_
69|
70|_"It hurts..."_
71|
72|_"Please..."_
73|
74|_"There's room for you too..."_
75|
76|These aren't ghosts wandering the forest. They are psychic echoes emanating from the Jars of Souls.
77|
78|---
79|
80|# 1. The Entrance
81|
82|A grassy clearing surrounds a large hill. Built into its base is an ancient stone doorway leading downward.
83|
84|Weathered stairs descend into darkness.
85|
86|Characters approaching within 30 feet hear faint whispers from below.
87|
88|A **DC 12 Intelligence (Arcana or Religion)** check reveals that these aren't ordinary haunting manifestations. Something beneath the hill is magically attracting or containing spirits.
89|
90|The stairs descend approximately 40 feet before reaching Area 2.
91|
92|---
93|
94|# 2. The Landing
95|
96|A circular chamber marks the true entrance to the complex.
97|
98|An enormous necromantic rune has been carved into the floor.
99|
100|Four stone pedestals surround it, each holding a grotesque idol depicting a forgotten entity devouring humanoid spirits.
101|
102|A successful **DC 12 Intelligence (Arcana or Religion)** check identifies the circle's purpose:
103|
104|**It channels spiritual energy toward the center of the tomb.**
105|
106|The large double doors leading to Area 7 have no handles or visible locks.
107|
108|Magic seals them.
109|
110|Casting _Detect Magic_ reveals strong Necromancy and Abjuration magic.
111|
112|The doors open only when someone speaks:
113|
114|**"Syvethis."**
115|
116|The characters can discover the command word in Area 6.
117|
118|Attempting to force the doors open automatically fails.
119|
120|---
121|
122|# 3. Immortal Guardians
123|
124|Two separate chambers contain one of Dopendis Gravebreath's earliest successful Jars of Souls each. These two jars are **inert**: they contain tortured souls, but they do not power the tomb's guardians or emit necrotic energy.
125|
126|Each room contains:
127|
128|- Two stone guardian statues
129|- One inert Jar of Souls
130|- Ancient necromantic inscriptions
131|
132|When a creature approaches within 10 feet of the jar, the statues animate.
133|
134|### Encounter
135|
136|Use **2 Animated Armors** in each room.
137|
138|However, the guardians aren't interested in pursuing intruders through the dungeon.
139|
140|They exist solely to protect the jar.
141|
142|If characters retreat from the chamber, the constructs return to their original positions after 1 minute.
143|
144|### The Inert Jar
145|
146|A black ceramic vessel rests upon a stone pedestal. Ghostly faces occasionally push outward from its surface before disappearing.
147|
148|Each inert jar contains a dark, viscous Arcannabis concentrate called **[[Soul Diesel]]**: trapped souls mixed with humanoid blood. The souls remain conscious within the mixture, which is why the liquid whispers with the voices Bongston heard after his companions died. A creature that touches the jar hears dozens of overlapping whispers, including fragments of the souls’ final memories. Unlike the active jars in Area 7, an inert jar is not connected to the ritual machinery and does not empower the undead.
149|
150|A creature that ingests a dose of Soul Diesel gains **1d4 bonus damage of the same type as its attack against humanoids** for 1 hour. The effect applies once per turn. Using the strain is disturbing and illegal in most civilized settlements, since its manufacture requires tortured souls and humanoid blood.
151|
152|Characters who accepted [[Skarguther Dungleboof]]’s [[The Roach Clip]] contract can identify this as the item he wants. He pays **100 gp for each intact inert jar** in Area 3 and **300 gp for each intact active jar** in the ritual chamber. The vessel must remain sealed and undamaged; a broken jar earns nothing. Characters who did not accept the contract can still recognize that the jar would interest collectors of forbidden magic, but selling it would be dangerous and morally fraught.
153|
154|This creates a clear choice. The characters can carry the jar to Skarguther, placing its tortured souls in the hands of a Duster who claims he can guide them toward [[Heralds of Dust|True Death]]. Or they can smash it, freeing the souls and allowing them to pass into the afterlife, but destroying the vessel and forfeiting its reward. They may choose differently for each jar, but Skarguther pays only for intact vessels.
155|
156|### Breaking an Inert Jar
157|
158|AC 12  
159|HP 10  
160|Immune: Poison, Psychic
161|
162|Destroying an inert jar releases the souls trapped inside, but because the vessel is disconnected from the ritual machinery, it does not produce the violent psychic backlash of an active jar. The spirits emerge as pale figures, briefly surround the characters, and then disappear. A character proficient in Arcana or Religion realizes that the souls have finally been allowed to pass into the afterlife.
163|
164|### Taking the Jar
165|
166|The characters may instead carry the intact vessel. It is heavy, fragile, and constantly whispers to anyone holding it. Wrapping it securely prevents accidental damage, but does not silence the voices.
167|
168|If the characters accepted Skarguther’s contract, they must transport the jar to the Dungsweepers’ mortuary offices in [[The Undercity Osslurraggath]] and present it to Skarguther or one of his Duster attendants to collect the reward. Otherwise, carrying it could attract the attention of necromancers, undead creatures, religious authorities, or [[Dopendis Gravebreath]].
169|
170|---
171|
172|# 4. Forsaken Sarcophagi
173|
174|Several sarcophagi line the corridors surrounding the central chamber.
175|
176|They initially appear dormant.
177|
178|They aren't.
179|
180|The tomb's guardians awaken whenever someone interferes with Dopendis Gravebreath's experiments.
181|
182|The **first time the characters move, damage, or destroy a Jar of Souls**, two nearby sarcophagi burst open.
183|
184|### Encounter
185|
186|**1d4 - 1 (min 1) Ash Zombies** emerge from the closest sarcophagi. The are 6 Ash Zombies total.
187|
188|Afterward, the remaining sarcophagi occasionally rattle or produce scratching sounds, but don't immediately open.
189|
190|When the characters eventually open the doors to Area 7, **the remaining Ash Zombies** emerge from their sarcophagi.
191|
192|This splits the original six-monster encounter into manageable battles while maintaining the feeling that the entire tomb is waking around them.
193|

# Adventure Summary

**Jars of Souls** is a tomb investigation adventure set in the wooded interior of [[The Outback]] beyond [[Doobius House]]. A newly revealed stone doorway has appeared beneath a grassy hill, and several explorers, hunters, and woodsmen who entered it never returned. The only survivor, [[Bongston Vale]], came back half-starved and raving about black jars filled with screaming souls.

The [[Free League of Stickyickistan]] needs licensed adventurers to investigate the tomb, recover evidence of its purpose, and determine what happened to the missing people. A scholar from [[N.E.R.D]] has also taken interest after comparing Bongston’s account to strange necromantic evidence recovered from [[Blacklung Quarry]].

# The Rolling Papers Advertisement

**Submitted by:** [[Free League of Stickyickistan]] / [[N.E.R.D]]  
**Tier:** Tier 1  
**Recommended Level:** 3  
**Expected Length:** One-shot, approximately 3–4 hours  
**Tone:** Tomb exploration, undead horror, occult mystery, moral choices, dark fantasy  
**Location:** [[Doobius House]] / [[The Outback]]

## Headline

> **NEWLY REVEALED TOMB BEYOND DOOBIUS HOUSE: LICENSED ADVENTURERS REQUESTED**

## Public Notice

A stone doorway has appeared beneath a grassy hill in the wooded interior beyond [[Doobius House]]. Several local explorers, hunters, and woodsmen entered the site after its discovery and never returned.

Their sole survivor, [[Bongston Vale]], is recovering at the [[FLS Guildhall]] and has given confused testimony about stone guardians, walking corpses, and black ceramic jars filled with screaming voices. Families of the missing have asked the Guildhall to learn what happened to their loved ones and, if possible, free any trapped souls found within.

A scholar from [[N.E.R.D]] offers payment for reliable evidence recovered from the tomb. The scholar suspects the site may be connected to a forbidden substance called **[[Soul Diesel]]**, but proof is needed from inside.

# The Roach Clip Tip

A coded notice may circulate among characters with ties to [[The Roach Clip]], the Dusters, or the events beneath [[Blacklung Quarry]]. An anonymous buyer is offering discreet payment for intact black soul-jars recovered from the tomb, with instructions to deliver them through the [[Dungsweepers]]’ mortuary offices in [[The Undercity Osslurraggath]].

This private offer conflicts with the families’ request to free the dead, creating a moral choice about whether the jars should be studied, sold, or destroyed.

# What Players Should Know

- **Content / vibe:** Tomb horror, trapped souls, undead, necromancy, occult laboratories, moral dilemmas, and dark fantasy.
- **Combat / roleplay / exploration mix:** Dungeon exploration with undead and construct combat, investigation, lore discovery, and choices about dangerous artifacts.
- **Character hooks:** Good for Free League contractors, tomb delvers, necromancer hunters, religious characters, scholars, Dusters, characters connected to [[The Tenebrous Stone-r]], or anyone with a reason to protect the dead from exploitation.
- **Special notes:** The adventure includes trapped souls and potentially valuable cursed objects. Characters may face competing incentives between public duty, private profit, and doing right by the dead.

# Rewards

- **1,200 XP each** for completing the adventure and resolving the fate of the trapped souls.
- **150 gp each** from the [[N.E.R.D]] scholar for investigating the tomb and returning with evidence.
- Possible private payment from a [[The Roach Clip]] buyer for intact jars recovered from the tomb.
- Additional treasure recovered from the dungeon.
- Possible bonus XP for rescuing or laying to rest the souls of the missing, and for recovering reliable evidence of necromantic experiments.

# Sign-Up

**DM:** Initiate of Tribulation, Vorg Lordcaster  
**Date / Time:** TBD  
**Seats:** 4–5 players  
**How to join:** Register through the [[FLS Guildhall]] / post in the Free League chat.

Got it. For **`Jars of Souls Player Brief.md`**, I’ll treat it as **player-facing only** and avoid including hidden DM information.

That means I should **not** include details like:

- Dopendis Gravebreath’s identity or role
- Orcus cult confirmation
- The mass raise dead ritual / Great Working
- Exact contents of the tomb
- Exact enemy types or encounter details
- Whether Soul Diesel is definitely present or how it works
- The full truth behind [[Blacklung Quarry]] connections
- Secret motives or identities behind private contracts, unless the players would plausibly see them in the notice

Player-safe information can include:

- The public job posting
- Rumors and survivor testimony
- The missing explorers from [[Doobius House]]
- That [[N.E.R.D]] suspects a connection to strange necromantic evidence
- That **[[Soul Diesel]]** is suspected, not confirmed
- General vibes/content warnings
- Public rewards and vague private/underground incentives

I’ll keep that distinction in mind for any future edits to the player brief.

      "content": "1|# Character Advancement
2|
3|Character advancement in the [[Free League of Stickyickistan]] is designed for an open-table campaign with rotating players, rotating DMs, and shared continuity. Characters grow by completing adventures, recording rewards, and carrying their reputation forward between sessions.
4|
5|## Advancement Method
6|
7|The FLS uses **XP per adventure**.
8|
9|Each adventure has a listed XP reward. When a character completes that adventure, they earn the listed XP and record it with their session rewards. XP is awarded for completing the adventure, not for individually counting every defeated monster, trap, or encounter.
10|
11|The listed XP reward may account for:
12|
13|- Expected combat encounters
14|- Investigation and exploration
15|- Major objectives
16|- Optional objectives
17|- Monster-hunting difficulty
18|- Adventure length
19|- Risk, complications, and consequences
20|
21|Characters level up when their total XP reaches the normal D&D level thresholds.
22|
23|## Adventure XP
24|
25|Adventure briefs and DM notes should list the expected XP reward for each character.
26|
27|Example:
28|
29|> **Rewards:** 225 gp each, 600 XP each
30|
31|## Partial Completion
32|
33|If the party does not complete the adventure, the DM may award partial XP based on meaningful progress.
34|
35|| Progress | XP Award |
36||---|---:|
37|| Minor progress | 25% of the adventure XP |
38|| Major progress, but objective incomplete | 50% of the adventure XP |
39|| Main objective complete, but major complications unresolved | 75% of the adventure XP |
40|| Adventure complete | 100% of the adventure XP |
41|
42|Partial XP is optional. If the party abandons the job, fails the main objective, or causes a disaster, the DM may reduce or withhold XP as appropriate.
43|
44|## Bonus XP
45|
46|Some adventures may offer bonus XP for optional objectives, exceptional problem solving, protecting civilians, rescuing NPCs, preserving important sites, capturing instead of killing, harvesting a dangerous monster cleanly, or preventing collateral damage.
47|
48|Bonus XP may be listed in the adventure rewards when possible.
49|
50|Examples:
51|
52|- +50 XP for rescuing a trapped NPC
53|- +100 XP for preserving a sacred site
54|- +150 XP for completing a clean monster harvest
55|- +250 XP for resolving a threat without starting a faction conflict
56|
57|## Session Length
58|
59|Session length helps determine how much XP an adventure should be worth, but characters do not automatically level after a four-hour session.
60|
61|A four-hour adventure usually counts as a **standard adventure** for XP purposes. Shorter sessions may award less XP, while longer or more dangerous adventures may award more.
62|
63|For multi-session adventures, the DM should tell players how XP will be awarded. Usually, XP is awarded at the end of the adventure or after a major milestone.
64|
65|## Suggested XP by Adventure Tier
66|
67|Use these values as a starting point when assigning XP to Free League adventures.
68|
69|| Adventure Type | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 | Tier 4 |
70||---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
71|| Short adventure / 2–3 hours | 300 XP | 1,500 XP | 5,000 XP | 12,000 XP |
72|| Standard adventure / 3–4 hours | 600 XP | 3,000 XP | 10,000 XP | 25,000 XP |
73|| Long adventure / 4–6 hours | 900 XP | 5,000 XP | 15,000 XP | 40,000 XP |
74|| Deadly or major adventure | 1,200 XP | 7,500 XP | 25,000 XP | 60,000 XP |
75|
76|DMs may adjust these values based on difficulty, objectives, party level, and how much progress the adventure represents.
77|
78|## Tier of Play
79|
80|Characters are grouped into broad tiers of play.
81|
82|| Tier | Character Levels | XP Range | Maximum Magic Item Rarity |
83||---|---:|---:|---|
84|| Tier 1 | 1–4 | 0–6,499 XP | Uncommon |
85|| Tier 2 | 5–10 | 6,500–63,999 XP | Rare |
86|| Tier 3 | 11–16 | 64,000–354,999 XP | Very Rare |
87|| Tier 4 | 17–20 | 355,000+ XP | Legendary |
88|
89|A character should generally play in adventures appropriate to their tier. DMs may set tighter level ranges for specific adventures.
90|
91|## Recording Advancement
92|
93|At the end of each session, players should record:
94|
95|- Adventure name
96|- Date played
97|- DM
98|- Character level before and after the session
99|- Total XP before and after the session
100|- XP earned
101|- Gold earned
102|- Magic items gained
103|- Consumables gained or spent
104|- Downtime, favors, faction changes, or story awards
105|- Any lasting conditions, curses, diseases, debts, or consequences
106|
107|Rewards should be recorded before leaving the table whenever possible.
108|
109|## Gold and Treasure
110|
111|Gold, treasure, and mundane equipment are awarded as directed by the adventure.
112|
113|If treasure is found during play, the party may use it during the session. At the end of the session, remaining treasure with monetary value is converted to gold and divided as the party desires.
114|
115|For guidance, total treasure by adventure tier should usually fall within these ranges:
116|
117|| Adventure Tier | Typical Total Treasure |
118||---|---:|
119|| Tier 1 | 100–500 gp |
120|| Tier 2 | 1,000–5,000 gp |
121|| Tier 3 | 10,000–50,000 gp |
122|| Tier 4 | 50,000–100,000 gp |
123|
124|## Magic Items
125|
126|Characters may keep magic items found during an adventure if the item is specifically awarded by the adventure or approved by the DM. Finding a magic item in and adventure doesn't necessarily mean you get to keep it afterwards.
127|
128|Items that are loaned to the party, required for an objective, destroyed by the story, or marked as temporary rewards cannot be kept unless the adventure says otherwise.
129|
130|Magic items should be appropriate to the character’s tier. If an adventure randomly awards an item above the tier’s maximum rarity, reroll it or replace it with an appropriate item.
131|
132|## Consumables
133|
134|Potions, scrolls, ammunition, Arcannabis products, monster components, and other consumables should be recorded when gained or spent.
135|
136|Consumables may be used during the adventure in which they are found unless the DM says otherwise. Any remaining consumables at the end of the session belong to the characters who receive them.
137|
138|## Story Awards
139|
140|Story awards represent favors, titles, access, faction standing, special permissions, curses, debts, or ongoing consequences.
141|
142|Examples include:
143|
144|- Trusted guest status at a location
145|- Access to a restricted shop, faction, or region
146|- A favor owed by an NPC
147|- Reputation with a guild or noble house
148|- A curse, mark, debt, or enemy
149|- A License or Recipe to craft a specific item from harvested monster parts that may be illegal or exceptionally rare.
150|
151|Story awards should be written clearly so future DMs know what they mean.
152|
153|## Downtime
154|
155|Characters may use downtime between or during sessions when the DM agrees there is enough time for the activity.
156|
157|Downtime can represent training, crafting, research, carousing, recovery, spell copying, faction work, business, or other between-adventure activity.
158|
159|The DM has final say on whether downtime is available during a specific adventure.
160|
161|## Death, Disease, and Curses
162|
163|Bad things happen to adventurers.
164|
165|Diseases, curses, poisons, and other lasting effects persist until removed by magic, downtime, story resolution, or the adventure’s conclusion. Characters may seek spellcasting services in settlements or through appropriate NPCs when available.
166|
167|If a character dies, follow the table rules for resurrection, replacement characters, or post-adventure recovery.
168|
169|## Player Responsibility
170|
171|Players are responsible for keeping their own character records accurate.
172|
173|DMs should clearly state rewards at the end of a session, but players should track what their character earned, spent, lost, and suffered.
174|
175|If a record is unclear, the current DM may make a fair ruling based on the available notes.

## Adventure Rewards

**900 XP each** for completing the adventure: recovering the stolen shipment, stopping the cult from restarting the Soul Diesel process, and deciding what becomes of the Ash Ledger. This is a long Tier 1 adventure reward under [[Character Advancement]].

**175 gp each** from the [[Free League of Stickyickistan]] for recovering the shipment and returning with reliable evidence of the cult’s activity. This payment is divided among the characters who complete the contract.

Additional rewards:

- **100 gp total** from [[N.E.R.D]] if the party turns over the Ash Ledger, intact alchemical notes, or other useful research evidence.
- **50 gp total** for recovering salvageable alchemical glassware or mining equipment from the stolen shipment.
- Any mundane equipment recovered from defeated cultists or the waystation, subject to DM approval.
- A story award for uncovering the cult’s attempt to rebuild the Soul Diesel operation after [[Sarbrindar]] and [[Dopendis Gravebreath]] were defeated or exposed.

Optional bonus XP:

- **+50 XP each** for capturing a cultist alive for questioning.
- **+50 XP each** for preserving the Ash Ledger instead of destroying it.
- **+100 XP each** for preventing any new Soul Diesel distillation from being completed.

If the characters complete only part of the adventure, use the partial-XP guidelines in [[Character Advancement]].

# The Ashen Choir

_A D&D 5e (2024) adventure for 4–5 4th-level characters_

A wave of faint, overlapping voices begins drifting through the lower tunnels of [[The Undercity Osslurraggath]]. The sounds are not loud enough for most citizens to hear, but priests, gravediggers, Dusters, and anyone who has handled necromantic relics describe the same thing: a choir of the dead, singing from somewhere beneath the old mortuary drains.

The disturbance can follow any earlier Orcus adventure, but does not require them to happen in a fixed order. If [[Sarbrindar]] has already been defeated, the voices are drawn to residue left by the quarry disaster. If [[Dopendis Gravebreath]]’s laboratory has already been exposed, they are drawn to the jars and Soul Diesel evidence recovered from the tomb. If [[The Last Batch]] has already happened, the choir is responding to the Ash Ledger and the interrupted shipment. If none of those events have occurred yet, the disturbance is simply one of the cult’s hidden backup rites beginning to fail on its own.

The characters must descend into abandoned funerary tunnels beneath the [[Dungsweepers]]’ mortuary, find the source of the singing, and decide whether to silence, preserve, or study the dead voices before the choir becomes strong enough to wake corpses across the district.

## Adventure Summary

1. The characters receive a public contract from the [[FLS Guildhall]] after citizens report disturbing voices beneath [[The Undercity Osslurraggath]]. Characters with Duster ties or previous Orcus-cult experience may also receive a private warning through [[The Roach Clip]].
2. They interview mortuary workers, Dusters, grieving families, and frightened tunnel crews to learn where the voices are loudest.
3. They explore the old mortuary drains beneath the [[Dungsweepers]]’ offices, avoiding unstable tunnels, corpse-water hazards, and minor undead stirred by the choir.
4. They discover a hidden reliquary chamber where the Orcus cult stored funerary nameplates, ashes, teeth, and scraps of death records stolen from multiple sites.
5. They confront the **Ashen Cantor**, a failed cult medium whose body is dead but whose voice continues conducting the trapped echoes of the dead.
6. They decide what to do with the choir: release the voices, preserve them as evidence, let the Dusters guide them toward [[Heralds of Dust|True Death]], or allow [[N.E.R.D]] to study the phenomenon.

## Modular Series Notes

This adventure should work whether it is played before or after [[The Tenebrous Stone-r]], [[Jars of Souls]], or [[The Last Batch]]. Do not require the same characters to have played the earlier sessions.

Use whichever hook fits the table:

- **After The Tenebrous Stone-r:** the choir reacts to death-energy residue carried out of [[Blacklung Quarry]].
- **After Jars of Souls:** the choir reacts to black jars, Soul Diesel samples, or notes brought back from the tomb beyond [[Doobius House]].
- **After The Last Batch:** the choir reacts to the Ash Ledger, which contains partial names of the dead stolen for the cult’s next rite.
- **Before any of them:** the choir is a separate cult cache breaking down, foreshadowing the larger Orcus network without revealing its full purpose.

## Adventure Rewards

**900 XP each** for completing the adventure: locating the source of the choir, preventing a mass undead outbreak in the district, and resolving the fate of the trapped voices. This is a long Tier 1 adventure reward under [[Character Advancement]].

**175 gp each** from the [[Free League of Stickyickistan]] for investigating the disturbance and returning with reliable evidence. This payment is divided among the characters who complete the contract.

Additional rewards:

- **100 gp total** from the [[Dungsweepers]] if the party prevents damage to the mortuary tunnels or recovers stolen funerary records.
- **100 gp total** from [[N.E.R.D]] if the party preserves safe evidence of the choir phenomenon without leaving the dead trapped.
- Any mundane equipment, ritual tools, or salvage recovered from the cult reliquary, subject to DM approval.
- A story award for earning the trust of local Dusters, the [[Dungsweepers]], or families whose dead were disturbed by the cult.

Optional bonus XP:

- **+50 XP each** for identifying at least one stolen name and returning it to the correct family or temple.
- **+50 XP each** for preventing collateral damage in the mortuary or surrounding Undercity tunnels.
- **+100 XP each** for resolving the choir without destroying recoverable evidence or leaving any voices trapped.

If the characters complete only part of the adventure, use the partial-XP guidelines in [[Character Advancement]].

---

## Best pick

### **The Zooka Mouth Correctional Crucible**

This is probably my favorite because it immediately says:

- near the mouth of Mount Zooka
- a prison
- unbearably hot
- designed to “reforge” criminals
- nasty enough for a prison break

Common names:

- **The Crucible**
- **Zooka Mouth**
- **The Mouth**
- **Correctional Crucible**

Example usage:

> [[Unit BH-Umbra Δ9]] has been arrested and transferred to **the Zooka Mouth Correctional Crucible**, a geothermal detention fortress built into the steaming vents near the mouth of [[Mount Zooka]].

### **The Cinderlock**
Short, punchy, memorable.

> The Cinderlock is a basalt-walled prison complex built into volcanic stone near [[Mount Zooka]], where heat, ash, and pressure do half the guards’ work for them.

### **Zooka Mouth Maximum**
A little more modern and stupid-funny.

More fantasy, less Stickyickistan absurdity.

> **The Sweatbox**

Very bureaucratic and silly.

That works better for a **Prisoner 13** conversion anyway, since the original remote frozen fortress vibe becomes usable again without keeping it on Toril.

Here are some names for a cold, mountainous detention center in the northernmost reaches of **Mythmos**:

## Best pick

### **Frostmaw Hold**

Short, fantasy-forward, and memorable. It sounds like a prison built into a mountain pass, glacier, or cliffside cave system.

> [[Unit BH-Umbra Δ9]] has been arrested and transferred to **Frostmaw Hold**, a remote mountain prison in the northernmost reaches of Mythmos, where ice, altitude, and distance are considered part of the security system.

## Other strong options

### **The Rimevault**

Feels like a place where dangerous people and secrets are stored forever.

> The Rimevault is carved into a frozen mountain deep in northern Mythmos, its cells sealed behind enchanted ice, iron doors, and killing winds.

### **Blackice Bastion**

Good if you want a harsher, more military fortress feel.

> Blackice Bastion squats above a glacier-fed ravine, a fortress-prison where the stone is slick with frozen mist and every escape route leads into white death.

### **The Northmost Gaol**

Simple, ominous, and old-world.

> The Northmost Gaol is less a prison than a sentence: a fortress at the edge of Mythmos where the mountains decide who survives long enough to stand trial.

### **Kaldspire Prison**

A proper-name fantasy prison, good if you want it to sound institutional.

> Kaldspire Prison rises from a jagged peak in northern Mythmos, its towers crusted with ice and its lower cells buried deep in the mountain.

### **The White Lock**

Very clean and ominous. Good nickname or official name.

> The White Lock holds prisoners no one wants to execute, release, or remember.

### **Glaciergate Penitentiary**

More formal.

> Glaciergate Penitentiary guards the only pass through a frozen mountain chain in northern Mythmos, making the prison and the pass one fortified chokepoint.

### **The Howling Bastille**

Evocative if wind and sound matter in the adventure.

> At night, the mountain winds scream through the barred vents of the Howling Bastille, masking footsteps, alarms, and sometimes murder.

## My recommendation

Use:

> **Frostmaw Hold**

It is the easiest to remember, sounds dangerous, and gives you strong environmental flavor without being too goofy.

Suggested replacement language for your intro:

> [[Unit BH-Umbra Δ9]], the first recognized Bloodhound squad of the [[Ashen Shadow Society Creature Utilisation & Neutralisation Taskforce]], has been arrested and transferred to **Frostmaw Hold**, a remote mountain prison in the northernmost reaches of Mythmos. The fortress is built into a frozen ridgeline where ice, altitude, and distance are considered part of the security system. The [[Ashen Shadow Society]] wants the squad back before its members, contacts, field notes, and recovered specimens become someone else’s property.

You could also give it a nickname:

- **The Maw**
- **The Hold**
- **The White Lock**
- **The Last Cell**
- **The Cold House**

My favorite full combo:

> **Frostmaw Hold**, called **the White Lock** by the people unlucky enough to be sent there.

For a cold northern Mythmos prison with a **subtle stoner vibe**, I’d avoid making the official name too jokey. Make the formal name intimidating, then let the nickname carry the weed pun.

## Best options

### **Frostbowl Hold**
My top pick.

It sounds like a frozen mountain basin, but “bowl” gives it a quiet stoner double meaning.

> **Frostbowl Hold**, called **the Bowl** by inmates, is a remote mountain prison in the northernmost reaches of Mythmos.

### **Rimebowl Bastion**
A little more fantasy.

> **Rimebowl Bastion** sits in a glacier-carved basin where the wind circles endlessly and no smoke rises straight.

### **The White Bowl**
More overt, but still subtle enough if played straight.

> **The White Bowl** is carved into a snow-choked mountain basin near the northern edge of Mythmos.

### **Highpine Hold**
Subtle, natural, and quietly smoky.

> **Highpine Hold** stands above the treeline in northern Mythmos, where the air is thin, cold, and impossible to hide in.

### **Frostleaf Gaol**
A little more weed-coded, but still fantasy.

> **Frostleaf Gaol** was named for the pale alpine plants that grow around its lower cliffs.

### **Kiefspine Keep**
More obvious, but still usable if your setting likes puns.

> **Kiefspine Keep** rises from a jagged ridge of pale stone and windblown powder.

### **The Greenlight Bastion**
A subtle prison/security phrase plus weed-adjacent “green.”

> **Greenlight Bastion** is named for the auroras that burn over its towers on clear winter nights.

### **The Glassy Peak**
Works if the prison is icy and slick, with “glassy” as a subtle intoxication nod.

> **The Glassy Peak** is less a fortress than a frozen sentence, a prison carved into black stone and blue ice.

## My recommendation

Use:

> **Frostbowl Hold**

Nickname:

> **the Bowl**

Possible intro text:

> [[Unit BH-Umbra Δ9]], the first recognized Bloodhound squad of the [[Ashen Shadow Society Creature Utilisation & Neutralisation Taskforce]], has been arrested and transferred to **Frostbowl Hold**, a remote mountain prison in the northernmost reaches of Mythmos. Built into a glacier-carved basin known to inmates as **the Bowl**, the fortress uses altitude, cold, and distance as part of its security system.

That gives you the stoner vibe without making the prison feel like a joke.

Prior to her incarceration years ago, Korda was an ally and agent of Clan Axebreaker, a moderately influential dwarf clan in a stronghold called Gauntlgrym. Korda built a network of informants and agents, ostensibly all to the benefit of Clan Axebreaker. With each success, she paid tattooists to inscribe a memorial of her triumph onto her skin. Using ancient rituals, Korda infused many of these artful etchings with the magic of Gauntlgrym’s forges, granting her wondrous gifts.

Korda grew too ambitious for her role as an agent, so she devised a plan to take power for herself. Over five years she took careful stock of Clan Axebreaker’s wealth and, in one fell swoop, used her network of lieutenants to steal away most of the clan’s gold, leaving only a pittance.

The Axebreaker dwarves discovered her almost immediately. They rounded up her agents, who either fought to the death or were executed. They captured Korda and interrogated her, but she never revealed the location of the stolen fortune, even under magical compulsion. The Axebreaker dwarves used their influence to have her sentenced to life in prison at Revel’s End. There, Clan Axebreaker was hopeful Korda would eventually break and reveal the location of the stolen wealth. This played right into Korda’s hands, since she had made copious enemies who can’t move against her while she’s incarcerated.

Korda, now known as Prisoner 13, prepared for her imprisonment by laying the groundwork for a new spy and criminal network, which cost her much of her stolen fortune. She now runs her operations from the prison. Using her magical tattoos, she telepathically coordinates agents throughout Faerûn and beyond, none of whom know the identity of their employer. As for what remains of the stolen Axebreaker wealth, it rests in an unmarked vault in the depths of Gauntlgrym, sealed by a magical lock that only the runic sequence tattooed on Korda’s right hand can open.

## Adventure Hooks

The [[Ashen Shadow Society]] needs [[Unit BH-Umbra Δ9]] extracted from [[Giantfrost Penitentiary]] before Mythmos authorities sell, dissect, extradite, or magically interrogate the taskforce. The Society cannot openly send its best operatives without admitting ownership of the prisoners, so the job is passed down to a support crew with just enough talent to be useful and just little enough status to be deniable.

Use one or more of these hooks to bring the 4th-level infiltrators into the operation:

**Support Squad Assignment.** The characters are members of an Ashen Shadow support squad. [[Zara Blackthorn]], [[Kezrin Malvek]], or another handler gives them the mission as a chance to prove they deserve recognition beyond errand work, corpse hauling, and disposable backup duty. Success could earn them real squad status. Failure means the Society never knew them.

**Bloodhound Bounty.** The Society frames the job as a recovery contract: bring back its missing Bloodhounds, their field notes, and any confiscated specimens taken from them at arrest. The infiltrators are promised payment, promotion, and first claim on minor salvage that the Society does not classify as restricted property.

**Inside Contact.** One of the prisoners gets a message out of Giantfrost Penitentiary through a smuggled tooth, a shed skin sample, a trained parasite, a coded prayer, or some other ASSCUNT field trick. The message reaches the Society with a short warning: the prison is preparing to move Unit BH-Umbra Δ9 somewhere worse.

**Expendable Test.** The Council of Shadows or the Enigmatic Quartet quietly uses the mission as a trial run for a new crew. The infiltrators are not told everything. They receive maps, aliases, and partial security notes, but the Society withholds enough information to see whether they can improvise under pressure.

**Personal Stake.** One or more infiltrators owe Unit BH-Umbra Δ9 a debt, trained under an ASSCUNT hunter, lost a friend during the arrest, or wants access to the taskforce’s creature-harvesting knowledge. The Society’s motives are profit-driven, but the characters may have more personal reasons to risk the prison.

> **SPRINGARDEN SEEKS LICENSED MONSTER HUNTERS AFTER FEY DISTURBANCE AT HOLY SHRINE**

The [Blossom Union](Blossom%20Union) seeks licensed adventurers for an urgent matter in the holy gardens of [Springwood](Springwood). Visitors have been warned away from [Springarden](Springarden) after a dangerous fey presence disrupted the shrine, injured caretakers, and disturbed the sacred waters.

Applicants should be prepared for unpredictable fey magic, delicate terrain, and a site whose caretakers would strongly prefer it remain intact. Once a party is formed, report to [The Loot Tavern](The%20Loot%20Tavern) and ask for [Threeflower](Threeflower), who will provide travel instructions and explain how to reach Springarden.

The Blossom Union offers payment to capable adventurers who can identify the threat, protect the shrine, and resolve the disturbance without unnecessary damage to the garden or its sacred pools.

- **Up to 600 XP each** for completing the adventure.
- **225 gp each** from the [Blossom Union](Blossom%20Union) for protecting Springarden and resolving the fey disturbance.
- Gratitude from the [Blossom Union](Blossom%20Union).
- Possible future access to [Springarden](Springarden) as trusted guests, assuming the shrine is preserved.
- The opportunity to harvest unusual monster components for crafting up to 3 bespoke Boss Monster magic items.
- Possible bonus XP for preserving the shrine, protecting the sacred pools, or rescuing injured Blossom Union members.

### 4 - Itsy Bitsy Spiders

The party inadvertently stumbles into a region of the forest controlled by a clan of ettercaps, who use the area to herd and care for spiders of all kinds. A few outcast driders have found a home here as well, far from the judgmental eyes of their former kin. To all these creatures, intruders are nothing but food, and the party is promptly attacked by ravenous arachnids looking to expand their larder.

Environment. Webs all over the ground and trees create difficult terrain in the area.

Consequences. The spiders prefer to eat their meals alive, and luckily for the party, they aren’t feeling too hungry at the moment. If the party falls in combat, they wake up 1d4 hours later, wrapped in webbing and strung from tree branches. A creature can escape from the webs with a successful VDC Strength check.

APL Composition

1st 2 swarms of spiders

2nd 1 giant spider, 2 swarms of spiders

3rd 1 ettercap, 2 swarms of spiders

4th 1 ettercap, 2 giant spiders

5th 2 ettercaps, 2 phase spiders

6th 1 drider, 2 giant spiders

15th 5 driders, 4 phase spiders

16th 6 driders, 4 phase spiders

5 - Gaia’s Teeth: Forest

The bandit group Gaia’s Teeth (see Recurring Encounters) make use of advanced arboreal techniques and camouflage to execute skilled ambushes from the boughs of high trees. They will gladly take a gold tithe, a minimum of 20 times the APL.

Forest Camouflage. The attackers are adapted to the terrain; each creature can take the Hide action as a bonus action on its turn.

APL Composition

1st 3 banditsσ, 2 pseudodragonsσ

2nd 3 flying snakesσ, 3 scoutsσ

3rd 2 flying snakesσ, 2 spies, 2 thugsσ

4th 2 banditsσ, 2 brown bearsσ, 1 druidσ

5th 3 druidsσ, 2 owlbearsσ

6th 2 bandit captainsσ, 2 wereboarsσ

7th 2 bandit captainsσ, 2 owlbearsσ, 1 shambling moundσ

8th 1 shambling moundσ, 3 spies, 2 wereboarsσ

9th 2 druidsσ, 1 giant apeσ, 2 owlbearsσ

10th 1 giant apeσ, 2 rangers*σ

17th 3 assassinsσ, 2 giant apesσ, 2 treantsσ

18th 3 rangers*σ, 3 treantsσ, 2 young green dragonsσ

19th 3 assassinsσ, 3 giant apesσ, 3 treantsσ

20th 2 assassinsσ, 4 rangers*σ, 3 treantsσ, 2 young green dragonsσ

*See Appendix C

6 - The Cinder Lords

A coalition of fiery creatures calling themselves the Cinder Lords has come together to find a new base of operations. The forest is in a spot suitable for their purposes, but must first be incinerated in order to make room for a mighty stronghold. They suffer no interlopers, and are ready for combat when the party encounters their forces.

Non-Combat Alternative. The only way to avoid combat with the Cinder Lords is to agree to aid them in their pursuits. If the party spends at least 2 hours starting fires to clear the way for a stronghold, the Cinder Lords allow them to leave and even pay them for their troubles with a sum of gold pieces equal to 50 times the APL. Doing this, however, may incur the wrath of other denizens of the forest.

APL Composition

5th 2 faerie-o’-fires*, 2 hell hound

6th 2 faerie-o’-fires*, 1 fire elemental

7th 1 faerie-o’-fire*, 1 fire elemental, 2 hell hound

8th 1 fire giant, 1 hell hound

9th 3 faerie-o’-fires*, 2 fire elementals

10th 2 fire elementals, 3 hell hound

11th 1 faerie-o’-fire*, 2 fire giants

12th 1 fire elemental, 1 fire giant, 1 young red dragon

13th 2 fire elementals, 1 fire giant, 1 young red dragon

16th 1 horned devil, 2 young red dragons

17th 2 fire giants, 3 horned devils

18th 3 horned devils, 2 young red dragons

20th 2 fire elementals, 1 fire giant, 4 horned devils

*See Appendix C

7 - Beware the Behirs

Fancying themselves serpentine tyrants, a family of behirs has made a lair in the forest, and enslaved several creatures to help them amass a hoard to rival those of legendary dragons. The behirs keep their servants on a short leash, accompanying them on their forays for treasure to prevent escape. The party runs into one or more behirs alongside their slaves, who attack to rob the adventurers of their valuables. If all the behirs are defeated, the humanoids surrender immediately.

Non-Combat Alternative. The behirs’ arrogance and desire to emulate dragons can be turned against them. A successful VDC Charisma (Persuasion) check convinces the behirs to let the party go if they can outsmart the would-be-draconic creatures. The behirs agree to a game of riddles, consisting of best-of-three contested Intelligence checks, or, at the GM’s discretion, a sudden-death format battle of wits between the GM and players in which the two sides take it in turns to posit riddles. If one of the behirs’ slaves stands a better chance than them, they are forced to play on the behirs’ behalf. If the party succeeds, they can leave freely. If not, combat ensues.

Consequences. If the party is defeated, the behirs appropriate all of their treasure and enslave them. An opportunity for escape might present itself when they’re sent on an expedition in the company of one of the serpentine monsters.

APL Composition

8 - Highway Robbery

A group of veteran adventurers, disillusioned with their lives and achievements, have turned to banditry for quick coin to fund their vices. The former adventurers resort to ambush tactics, and creatures with a passive Perception score lower than the VDC are surprised. They fight to the death, and don’t pull any punches; if their foes are slain during the fight, then they never deserved to live in the first place.

Non-Combat Alternative. Despite their ruthlessness, these former adventurers are also practical and would rather not break a sweat if they don’t have to. They will gladly let the party go if their demands for loot are met. They will take a tithe in gold pieces equal to 200 times the APL, or a number of uncommon or rarer magic items equal to the party’s average proficiency bonus.
